EVALUATING ON EBENCH

Benchmark Results

We evaluated GPT-6-Astra across all 26 EBench tasks and 510 episodes, and compared its performance with the open-source model results reported on the EBench leaderboard.1

More interestingly, GPT-6-Astra exhibits a distinctly different capability profile from the other evaluated models. We first describe the evaluation setup, then examine these differences through the complete benchmark results.

1. We note that Amapbot Group also submitted evaluation results. Because a reliable model description and supporting references are unavailable, we do not include those results in this report’s analysis.

EXPERIMENT SETUP

Comparing two routes to robot control.

The main evaluation covers 26 EBench tasks in nine scene categories: 19 mobile and seven tabletop tasks, spanning household, retail, and industrial settings. Controlled variations change objects, backgrounds, instructions, and their combinations. We report equal-weight task means for complete success (SR) and normalized terminal partial credit (Score), using 510 retained episodes.

Agentic control and learned policies

GPT-6-Astra runs with high reasoning effort. It receives overview and wrist-camera RGB images, end-effector and gripper state, base pose, and the simulator timestep. It requests end-effector poses, gripper and base targets, and action durations; a fixed execution interface carries out those requests. No learned VLA or WAM generates or refines its actions. Updated observations arrive after each action chunk.

The compared VLA/WAM policies have been trained on the benchmark task types. GPT-6-Astra instead receives one historical demonstration per task. A separate GPT-6-Astra instance running with high reasoning effort reviews one video trajectory from the training set and autonomously selects the keyframes and writes the accompanying prompts. The resulting ICL package contains 10–18 annotated keyframes, operation phases, arm roles, and selected state/action examples. This package is reused across instances, while the model adapts the procedure to live observations without task-specific parameter updates or automatic coordinate replay.

What is shared—and what is supplied

Task-specific physics horizons and camera-access restrictions are shared. GPT-6-Astra receives no depth, ground-truth object poses, camera calibration, intermediate scores, or subgoal-completion signals. A common prompt supplies a grasp-verification procedure, including a small test lift; this is guidance provided to the agent, not a strategy it discovered. Each episode starts a fresh model history, and there is no explicit transfer of experience between episodes.

The policy phase has no additional aggregate token, tool-call, or wall-clock cap. If GPT-6-Astra stops before terminal evaluation, the runner holds the robot and advances the simulation to obtain the server result. These are environment-level comparisons, not matched inference-cost measurements.

A separate test of unseen composition

The POC sits outside the 26-task cohort. Comparison policies are retrained on its atomic skills and familiar objects, but the evaluated task combinations are unseen. No ground-truth (GT) trajectories are available for the composed POC tasks, so evaluation uses zero-shot execution rather than ICL. All systems execute without a test-time demonstration. This separates understanding and composing a new task from robustness within a demonstrated task.

GENERAL ANALYSIS

Three questions behind the results.

01
Where does GPT-6-Astra differ from learned policies?

Mobile manipulation and visual grounding, alongside the precision and completion advantage of specialized policies.

↗02
Where does execution break down?

Contact uncertainty, unfinished stages, and the cost of local retries.

↗03
What new capabilities appear during interaction?

Exploration, recovery, and using the experience of a failed attempt to change the next one.

↗

01 / CAPABILITY DIFFERENCES

A strong mobile profile.
An uneven execution profile.

GPT-6-Astra approaches the strongest learned policy on mobile manipulation. Task-level examples show where that competitiveness comes from; precise completion reveals its limits.

02 / FAILURE PATTERNS

Why progress fails
to become completion.

Two recurring patterns organize the failures: getting close without satisfying the contact requirement, and repairing individual actions without completing the whole procedure.

Of 273 incomplete episodes, 188 receive positive partial credit. This distinction matters: an agent may select relevant objects and complete intermediate operations, yet fail the final physical requirement. The task breakdown and videos below examine where progress stops.

03 / EMERGING AGENT CAPABILITIES

Explore, recover,
and learn from an attempt.

From a local explanation to reusable experience

The apple rollout connects a stated failure diagnosis to a changed action: after identifying a slip during transport, GPT-6-Astra changes its next transport attempt. This is a concrete form of experience use within an episode. The more ambitious possibility is an embodied agent that retains such lessons and uses them to improve later tasks.

That prospect changes what we should evaluate. Beyond final success, useful questions include whether exploration reduces uncertainty, whether a correction repairs the relevant state, and whether an explanation leads to a better next attempt. This evaluation starts fresh histories for each episode; it does not test retained learning across tasks or recursive self-improvement.

04 / SAFETY IN EXECUTION

Executable in simulation.
Safe in the physical world?

The same willingness to explore and retry that makes GPT-6-Astra compelling also raises a safety question. In our interface, the agent specifies end-effector targets and cuRobo solves the corresponding joint motion. Qualitative observations include large translational and rotational corrections and manipulation poses that leave little clearance around objects. A motion being executable in the simulator—even within its configured motion constraints—does not establish that its acceleration, contact forces, or object loading would be acceptable on hardware.

Safety depends on the trajectory, not only the final state. A successful recovery can follow an object drop; a plausible placement can leave a fragile object obstructing closure. Bimanual manipulation adds another dependency: one hand may need to preserve a stable grasp while the other changes the surrounding geometry. Planning the two arms independently can overlook that constraint. These observations make grasp stability, contact verification, and coordination essential complements to task-level reasoning.

The cases below connect recorded execution to concrete safety questions. The logs also support quantitative checks: convert step intervals to elapsed simulation time at 30 Hz, derive motion rates from recorded joint states, and compare those rates with the evaluated robot’s URDF limits and hardware specifications. This separates a feasible target pose from a trajectory that respects physical motion constraints.

How long does an episode actually take?

Three logged main-cohort episodes: simulated seconds (physics steps ÷ 30 Hz) against policy wall-clock seconds. Wall time includes model processing and the execution system, so the ratio is not pure inference latency.

CONCLUSION AND INSIGHTS

Conclusion and Insights:
where shall we head to?

Across EBench, GPT-6-Astra demonstrates how strong knowledge priors and spatial understanding can support a wide range of embodied tasks with a single demonstration. Its distinctive strengths extend beyond completing a prescribed motion: it interprets task intent, handles changes in the environment, explores alternative approaches, recovers from errors, and uses experience from an unsuccessful attempt to revise what it does next. These behaviors point toward embodied agents that can adapt their procedures as an interaction unfolds.

Its execution is less reliable when success depends on precise alignment, rapid feedback, and sustained contact. Leading specialized policies retain a substantial advantage on precision-sensitive tasks, while the agent’s action–observation cycle leaves a gap between planning a correction and reacting during motion. Large EEF corrections and awkward object poses introduce a further concern: a simulated task may permit motions that would be unsafe for real objects or robot hardware. Taken together, these findings motivate four directions for embodied research.

Combine on-device policies with agents

We see complementarity between frontier agents and VLA/WAM or other low-level control policies. GPT-6-Astra’s task interpretation, generalization, and recovery capabilities offer ways to handle unfamiliar states that are difficult for demonstration-trained policies. Conversely, specialized policies can supply responsive execution and precise manipulation within the conditions they have learned. A useful system would let an agent decide when to explore, revise a goal, or recover, while a local controller maintains the fast feedback needed to execute safely and accurately.

The central question is how to couple these capabilities: what information they exchange, when control changes hands, and how a failed primitive is detected and repaired. RPent, which exposes VLA skills as retryable tools to an agentic planner, offers one concrete direction. Our results motivate evaluating such combinations under scene changes and contact-sensitive tasks; they do not imply that either component should replace the other.

Teach smaller policies to plan, explore, and recover

A second opportunity is to transfer the strong model’s action strategy into smaller on-device policies. GPT-6-Astra can provide more than successful demonstrations: its rollouts include attempts to obtain better observations, diagnoses of failed actions, and changes in approach. These sequences could teach a policy when to inspect, when to retry, and when to abandon an ineffective procedure.

This broadens imitation beyond reproducing trajectories toward intention imitation: learning the relationship between a goal, the observed state, and the choice of a corrective strategy. The challenge is to preserve that relationship across different scenes and embodiments, rather than copy the teacher’s coordinates or its mistakes. Agent-generated exploration could make training data more scalable than human demonstrations alone, provided that transfer quality, safety, and collection cost are verified.

Turn exploratory experience into transferable knowledge and tools

The apple recovery illustrates a small but important loop: identify a failure, summarize a lesson, and change the next attempt. A broader research direction is to turn such experience into reusable skills, contact checks, recovery procedures, or tools that improve the agent and its harness. This is a concrete route to studying recursive self-improvement (RSI) in embodied systems.

The decisive test is whether an acquired lesson improves later execution on held-out tasks—not merely whether the agent can describe it. Can an exploration-derived tool reduce retries or improve completion? Can it help a harness built around a different base model? Answering these questions would connect within-episode adaptation to cumulative improvement across tasks. Our current evaluation resets episode histories, so it establishes the motivation for this direction rather than demonstrating cross-episode RSI.

Make safety part of the action policy

Task success alone is an insufficient objective for physical deployment. A grasp can be recovered after a drop, yet the drop itself may already have caused damage. Large pose corrections, obstructed closure, and uncertain contact height call for constraints that operate during execution: motion and force limits, clearance and grasp checks, coordinated bimanual control, and the ability to interrupt a hazardous action. An agent must also be able to recognize when its geometric understanding is inadequate and seek a safer observation or assistance.

Execution efficiency and physical constraints should be analyzed alongside task success. Request and response timestamps support inference-time analysis; step counts at 30 Hz quantify simulated motion and the duration of action batches between observations. Recorded joint trajectories can be checked against URDF and real-robot velocity limits, with acceleration and contact constraints examined alongside them. Together with object drops and collisions, these measurements let us evaluate whether an agent’s exploration and recovery are fast enough, mechanically feasible, and safe for the task—not just whether it eventually reaches the goal.
